content.text: John Evelyn’s diary (1677–1690) records journeys between London, Sayes Court, Wotton, Windsor, Portsmouth, Greenwich, Lambeth, Althorpe, Cashiobury, and many country estates. He describes gardens, libraries, churches, museums, scientific experiments, music, architecture, paper-making, military technology, and Royal Society affairs. He mourns the deaths of Mrs. Godolphin, Lord Ossory, and his children Mary and Elizabeth. The diary chronicles the Popish Plot, political trials and executions, religious persecution in France, James II’s Catholic policies, the Bishops’ acquittal, the Dutch invasion, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688–89. Evelyn repeatedly expresses Anglican convictions, moral anxiety, gratitude to God, and concern for national instability.
